# Thin basement membrane nephropathy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Glomerular diseases > Thin basement membrane nephropathy*

[Original Article Link](/library/xL0E-g)

---

## Summary

Thin <u>basement membrane</u> nephropathy is a primary <u>glomerulonephritis</u> caused by abnormalities of type IV <u>collagen</u> and thinning of the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>. Patients typically present with episodes of intermittent <u>gross hematuria</u> and flank <u>pain</u>, often triggered by <u>upper respiratory tract</u> (URT) infections or exercise. <u>Urinalysis</u> shows persistent <u>microhematuria</u> and sometimes <u>proteinuria</u>. <u>Kidney biopsy</u> is required for diagnosis, showing diffuse thinning of the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>. While the disease generally has an excellent prognosis and often does not require treatment, patients with <u>proteinuria</u> should be treated with <u>ACE inhibitors</u> to slow progression.

---

## Pathophysiology

* Abnormalities of type IV <u>collagen</u> cause thinning of the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u> → transient ruptures of <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillary</u> wall → <u>hematuria</u>

---

## Diagnosis

Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation and a <u>family history</u> of benign <u>hematuria</u>. <u>Renal biopsy</u> is reserved for patients with signs of progressive disease (e.g., <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>hyperkalemia</u>) and unclear <u>family history</u>.




* <u>Urinalysis</u>

* Usually only persistent <u>microhematuria</u>

* Possible episodic <u>gross hematuria</u>, potentially associated with <u>hypercalciuria</u> and <u>hyperuricosuria</u>

* Minor <u>proteinuria</u> is possible, especially in adults

* <u>Renal biopsy</u> 

* <u>Light microscopy</u>: no abnormalities

* <u>Electron microscopy</u>: diffuse thinning of the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>
